newsitem.title: JAPAN: HORSE RACING-SPORT OF KINGS BOOMS IN JAPAN.
newsitem.headline: HORSE RACING-SPORT OF KINGS BOOMS IN JAPAN.

text.p: Times are changing for the better in the horse racing industry in Japan.

With a 1995 betting turnover of $36 billion, over 85 percent of it off-course, and slight growth even during a declining economy, the Sport of Kings has now become the pleasure of the masses as over 26 million racegoers find a horse to cheer each year.
Racing officials forecast the sport's popularity can only grow further as new types of racegoers emerge and the quality of racing improves to world class.
Horse racing in modern Japan has gone through three phases.
During the years before World War two, racing was viewed as an elite sport with royalty and rich landowners and business people the main patrons.
For decades after the war, racetracks became a gambling haunt for gangsters and the newly rich.
As the 21st century approaches, the sport has evolved into good, clean Japanese family-style fun.
Shuji Inada, general manager of the Japan Association for International Horse Racing (JAIR), feels the sport has finally come of age.

"The courses have received heavy investment and their facilities have been upgraded to the best in the world," he said. "Racing has become much more than gambling. It is now leisure entertainment -- a place to take your wife and kids out for the day."
Even the fashionable young women of Tokyo are flocking to courses and racetracks have become a favourite place to take a date.

Horse racing is saddled with two authorities, the Japan Racing Association (JRA) which administers major tracks and the National Association of Racing (NAR), controlled by local governments, for regional racing.
At the popular provincial racecourses, attendance is high, almost on level with JRA, but betting is relatively low, under 20 percent of JRA's take and most of it bet at the track.
Pressure from international racing organisations is steadily pushing the sport to open more to competition from foreign horses, owners, trainers and jockeys.
The Japan Cup is firmly on the international scene as one of the sport's top races, although the World Cup in Dubai, being run next Saturday, is now the richest race in the calendar.
Deregulation is in motion, leaving racing authorities with the delicate challenge of protecting domestic concerns and at the same time opening up courses to global interests.

"By 1999, 55 percent of the races in Japan will be open for unraced horses from abroad and the current seven major races open to overseas competition will be raised to 12," said JAIR President Kinji Ogawa.

"Of course we want to see foreign jockeys in Japan and we'll be issuing three month licences for five jockeys at a time. But helping to guard the interests of Japanese breeders, owners, trainers and jockeys is an important task," he added.

Although tough bureaucratic regulations have helped the sport regain its good reputation, the rules have also held back natural growth, nowhere more obviously than in the way a surplus of owners are having problems finding a trainer whose numbers are limited by officialdom.
"Wanting to own a race horse for either status or as an investment has become very popular," said Sandra Mori, an American writer who has a horse farm outside Tokyo.
"But you can't get a good trainer or jockey so easily -- they're so busy."
According to one racing journalist, not only are trainers scarce, but some of them are using outdated methods.
"There's a lot of dead wood that needs cutting out," the journalist said.
The relatively low price and quality of foreign racehorses are also causing big problems for Japanese breeders.
With the weakening of the yen and the best bloodlines of Europe, the United States, and Australia up for sale, "Made in Japan" horses do not sell well.
In the 1970s there were about 3,500 breeders. Today, less than 2,000 are in the game.
But JAIR's Ogawa sees a silver lining.
With purchases such as Sunday Silence (Kentucky Derby winner) and various high class performers from Europe, some of the world's top racing blood now stands at stud in Japan.
"Japanese breeders must be able to resell such wonderful stock back to the U.S. and Europe in order to improve world bloodlines," Ogawa said.
"Selling back to Kentucky the best offspring of the famous horses we've brought is something to aim for."
